title: Are You Using This Power Word? -power-word/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin opens with a story about being stopped from bringing a banana into a football stadium and, unsatisfied with the guard's answer of 'it's our policy,' tracing his own curiosity back to research by psychologist Robert Cialdini showing that people comply far more readily with requests when given a reason, introduced by the word 'because.' He applies this finding to classroom management, arguing that even when enforcing rules through mandatory consequences rather than requests, students are far more likely to accept and internalize a consequence when a teacher follows a consistent three-step process: state the consequence, name the rule broken, and give a compelling reason using the word 'because.' He notes that Cialdini's research found that even weak or near-absurd reasons increased compliance, suggesting the word itself carries persuasive weight, though he still recommends offering reasons that genuinely make sense to students. He argues that skipping this explanatory step creates unnecessary friction and resentment when students are sent to consequences like time-out without understanding why, whereas explaining reasons is less confrontational and builds buy-in. The piece frames this simple linguistic habit as a research-backed lever for making an existing classroom management plan more effective without changing its substance.
points: Psychologist Robert Cialdini's research shows people comply far more readily with requests when given a reason introduced by the word 'because,' even when the reason offered is weak.
A recommended three-step method for enforcing classroom rules: state the consequence, name the rule broken, then give a compelling reason using 'because.'
Explaining reasons for consequences is less confrontational than issuing consequences without explanation, reducing friction and resentment between teacher and student.
If students are angry or complaining after being sent to a consequence like time-out, it often signals the teacher skipped explaining the underlying reason.
Classroom management does not need to be dictatorial to be effective, but it does benefit from being deliberately 'smart' about how rules and reasons are communicated.
quotes: I was eating a banana as I began to push through the turnstile, when a man in a red windbreaker, presumably security, stopped me and said, “Sir, you can’t bring that banana into the stadium.
As it turns out, that something has strong implications when it comes to classroom management and can possibly be the difference between success and failure with your students.

Dr. Robert B. Cialdini describes several experiments that prove overwhelmingly that when we ask someone to do something—or not to do something—the response will be much more favorable if we provide a compelling reason.
It’s interesting to note, however, that experimenters discovered that even when the reasons offered were poor—to the point of absurdity—most subjects were still agreeable to the request.

If your students go to time-out and are angry with you or are complaining about your decision, then you’re doing something wrong. Often, it’s because you’re not using the word because and then following with cogent reasons.
Classroom management doesn’t have to be demanding or dictatorial to be effective—and it shouldn’t be—but it does need to be smart.
